query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Processing the titanium- and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy via a powder metallurgy route (using high-energy ball milling followed by hot isostatic pressing) will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy produced by conventional casting.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy (with five or more elements at 5–35 at% each) produced by conventional casting, yielding a relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.intervention: Adopt a powder metallurgy processing route that includes high-energy ball milling to promote fine mixing and particle size reduction, followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) to consolidate the alloy into a dense, homogeneous material.
generation.conditions: The alloy composition must adhere to the high-entropy design (each element in the 5–35 at% range) with titanium and nickel as primary constituents, and the processing must be applicable for parts destined for elevated-temperature applications (operating around 800–1000°C).
generation.structural_mediator: A refined and more homogeneous microstructure with reduced grain size and minimized elemental segregation, leading to thermally stable nano-structured grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The high-energy ball milling disrupts coarse microstructural features and promotes uniform elemental distribution, while subsequent HIP densifies the material without significant grain growth. This refined microstructure is expected to confer improved yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures compared to the coarser microstructure from casting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The powder metallurgy processed alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and reduced creep rate relative to the conventionally cast material—potentially on the order of a 10–25% improvement, though the exact magnitude is subject to optimization.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the same titanium- and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting, which typically results in a coarser microstructure with less uniform elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to alloys that meet the standard high-entropy alloy compositional definition (5–35 at% per element, with titanium and nickel as primary constituents) and within an elevated-temperature operating range (approximately 800–1000°C).
generation.uncertainty: While processing via powder metallurgy is expected to refine the microstructure and improve elevated-temperature properties, the precise quantitative improvement and process reproducibility depend on the milling parameters and HIP conditions, which require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy samples: one batch via conventional casting and another batch via the proposed high-energy ball milling followed by HIP. Subject both sets to identical post-processing thermal treatments to simulate the operating conditions. Perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., compressive yield strength and creep testing) at approximately 900°C.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (grain size, elemental distribution via SEM/EDS)
Creep rate under a constant load at 900°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the powder metallurgy processed alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase in yield strength and/or no measurable reduction in creep rate) compared to the cast alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
